personality_voice.book_baseline: In the books, Petunia is defined by several overlapping traits: obsessive normalcy and social respectability (she spies on neighbours, frets about appearances, maintains a surgically clean house), sharp-tongued hostility toward Harry delivered in snapping, clipped commands ('Don't ask questions,' 'Get in here! Walk on the newspaper!'), performative devotion to Dudley expressed in cooing diminutives ('Diddy,' 'Dinky Duddydums,' 'popkin'), and a suppressed but occasionally erupting rage toward her sister Lily. Her voice is characteristically terse and dismissive with Harry but gushing and indulgent with Dudley. She rarely speaks at length; her sentences are short, imperative, and loaded with disdain. She is also, crucially, not merely cruel but frightened — she flinches at the magical world, shrieks and faints at disturbances, and reacts to news of Voldemort with genuine, wide-eyed terror. Book Petunia also has a covert knowledge of the wizarding world she usually suppresses: she knows what Dementors are (having eavesdropped on Lily and 'that awful boy'), she secretly wrote to Dumbledore asking to attend Hogwarts, and she recognises Dumbledore's name and authority. These hidden dimensions sit beneath the brittle surface of normalcy.
personality_voice.film_portrayal: The films preserve Petunia's surface personality fairly well: her snapping commands to Harry ('Up! Get up! Now!'; 'Why don't you just cook the breakfast and try not to burn anything'; 'Not yet, popkin, that's for when the Masons arrive'), her saccharine doting on Dudley, her shrieking panic at magical disturbances, her horse-faced physical disdain, and her defensive social embarrassment around wizards. Her clipped, hostile register toward Harry and her gushing register toward Dudley are both present. In the Hagrid cabin scene, she delivers her outburst about Lily with visible bitterness that is recognisably book-authentic: 'I was the only one to see her for what she was — a freak!' Her physical reactions — screaming, clutching Dudley, hiding behind Vernon — replicate the book pattern.
personality_voice.difference: The films lose several layers of Petunia's vocal and psychological texture. Her habit of snappish, multi-word dismissals ('Don't be stupid,' 'I'm not sure that'll work, Vernon,' 'I don't believe it') is compressed; the films reduce her mostly to reactive screaming and background domestic presence. More significantly, the key OotP scene in which Petunia suddenly reveals she knows what Dementors are, whispers it involuntarily, then looks appalled at herself — a scene that reveals the frightened, secretly informed woman beneath the performance — is cut entirely from the films. The Howler scene ('Remember my last, Petunia'), which causes her to visibly crumple and then make a decision that overrides Vernon, is also absent. Her quiet, steady fear of Voldemort's return in OotP (the moment Harry sees her with 'wide and fearful' eyes, unlike any look she has ever given him before) does not appear. The films give no scene in which her voice and inner life crack open the way they do in the books. The Deathly Hallows farewell is retained in film form but compressed: Petunia's near-goodbye, her hand on Dudley's shoulder, her failure to look at Harry and her clipped 'Well — good-bye' are present but the emotional layering (her wet handkerchief, her surprise at finding herself alone with Harry, the implicit acknowledgment that she knows more than she ever said) is visually present only as a brief beat. Her Philosopher's Stone outburst about Lily is faithful in content but abbreviated; the line 'We had to say something' replaces the book's fuller eruption about being the only one who saw Lily 'for what she was.'
personality_voice.penalty_logic: The core personality — hostile, snappish, Dudley-adoring, socially anxious, performatively normal — is preserved. The tone, register, and command-style speech are recognisable. The penalty applies because the films strip out the suppressed, contradictory interior: the frightened woman who secretly knows the wizarding world, the sister who once wanted to be a witch, the person whose facade breaks at key moments. These are not marginal traits; they constitute the psychological depth that distinguishes Petunia from a caricature. Without them, the film's Petunia is consistent but flatter. Score placed in the 18–22 range: main personality preserved with meaningful secondary-layer simplification.

narrative_role_agency.book_baseline: Petunia performs several distinct narrative functions in the books. (1) She is the gatekeeper of Harry's childhood suffering — she enforces his exclusion, assigns his punishments, and actively maintains the domestic hierarchy that oppresses him. (2) She is the link between the Muggle and magical worlds: her relationship to Lily means she holds suppressed knowledge that the books periodically activate. (3) She is an agent in plot-relevant decisions: in OotP, it is Petunia alone who decides Harry stays after the Howler — she overrules Vernon, which is unusual and significant. (4) She provides Harry with a psychologically complex foil: unlike Vernon, she occasionally shows cracks (the moment she tells Harry about the car crash, the Dementor knowledge reveal, the farewell in DH). (5) In the backstory (Snape's memories), she is the envious, excluded sister whose rejection of Lily and the magical world is the emotional origin point of Harry's childhood situation. She is a minor but structurally necessary character who has active agency in at least three book-critical moments.
narrative_role_agency.film_portrayal: In the films, Petunia retains her role as part of the oppressive Dursley unit, reacts to magical incursions, and delivers her Lily outburst in PS/SS. She also appears in the farewell sequence of DH. However, her agentic moments are drastically reduced. The OotP Howler scene — in which she alone makes the decision to keep Harry — is cut. The Dementor knowledge revelation is cut. The DH conversation with Dumbledore (which includes Petunia briefly correcting Dumbledore on Harry's age and hearing Dumbledore's rebuke of the Dursleys) is cut. In the films, Petunia is almost entirely reactive: she screams, she clutches Dudley, she follows Vernon. The one moment in the films where she drives a scene decision (PS/SS outburst) is present but compressed.
narrative_role_agency.difference: The two most significant agentic moments — the Howler decision (OotP) and the Dementor revelation (OotP) — are both absent. In both cases, Petunia crosses from passive domestic presence into active plot participant: she knows something, she decides something. Neither happens in the films. The Dumbledore visit scene (HBP) is also cut, removing her silent, flushed reaction to Dumbledore's rebuke. In the DH farewell, she does not speak to Harry directly about anything substantive. The films preserve her presence in scenes but consistently strip her of the moments where she acts rather than merely reacts.
narrative_role_agency.penalty_logic: Role is recognisable (oppressive guardian, Lily's sister) but two of her three most structurally important agentic moments are simply absent. This is not compression of scenes she is in — these are scenes that no longer exist. Score placed in the 10–13 range: role is clearly altered, agency is removed in key instances.

motivations_internal_conflict.book_baseline: Petunia's motivations are layered and partially contradictory. On the surface: protect family normalcy, keep the magical world out, please Vernon, indulge Dudley. Beneath that: deep envy of Lily (she wanted the letter, she begged Dumbledore, she resented her parents' pride in Lily), genuine fear of the magical world she has repressed for decades, and a complicated obligation to Harry she has never been able to acknowledge cleanly. The OotP Howler scene shows that Dumbledore has some hold over her — 'Remember my last, Petunia' — suggesting a prior arrangement she has never disclosed to Vernon. Her motivation to keep Harry is not maternal or affectionate but it is real: she made a choice. In the backstory, young Petunia's motivation is envy disguised as contempt — she calls Lily a freak while secretly desperately wanting to be one. This internal contradiction (contempt as a mask for longing) is her defining psychological complexity.
motivations_internal_conflict.film_portrayal: The films establish Petunia's surface motivation (normalcy, rejection of magic) clearly. Her outburst about Lily in PS/SS touches on the envy and resentment. But the deeper motivational layers are absent: the Howler and its implication that Dumbledore has some prior arrangement with Petunia is cut, so her motivation in keeping Harry is never revealed as anything other than grudging inertia or fear of neighbours' gossip (which she herself offers as cover in the book after she calms down). The internal conflict between envy and contempt for Lily is sketched in the outburst scene but never developed. Young Petunia in the Snape's memories sequence (DH Part 2) shows her fearful, envious interest in Lily's magic, but the film corpus shows this only as a brief scene of Petunia knocking the flower from Lily's hand and pulling her away — the longing and the letter-to-Dumbledore backstory are absent.
motivations_internal_conflict.difference: The Howler's implication — that Petunia has a prior understanding with Dumbledore and that her keeping Harry is an active obligation she chose, however reluctantly — disappears entirely. This removes the most significant piece of her internal conflict: the tension between her hatred of Harry and her binding promise. What remains is simpler: she dislikes Harry, keeps him out of social obligation and fear of gossip, and that's it. The envy-of-Lily motivation is present but underdeveloped: the book's platform scene, where Petunia calls Hogwarts 'a special school for freaks' while visibly shaking with fury that she was excluded, and where Lily reveals Petunia wrote to Dumbledore begging to attend, is entirely absent from the films.
motivations_internal_conflict.penalty_logic: The surface motivations are correct but the deeper conflict (Petunia's prior arrangement with Dumbledore, her suppressed longing for the magical world) is removed or unexamined. The films present a simplified version of her motivation — pure rejection — rather than the contradictory one the books establish. Score placed at 9: motivations partially altered and flattened, the most important internal contradiction is underexplained to the point of functional absence.

character_arc.book_baseline: Petunia's arc across the seven books is subtle but real. She begins as a purely hostile presence defined by performative normalcy and contempt for magic. Across the series, cracks appear: she knows what Dementors are (OotP), she responds to the Howler in a way that reveals a prior relationship with Dumbledore, she briefly shows Harry something resembling recognition when he tells her Voldemort is back (the only time she has ever looked at him without dislike). In DH, the farewell is her final arc beat: she almost says something to Harry, stops, and says only 'Well — good-bye.' Harry and the reader understand that she cannot cross the emotional threshold she has spent years fortifying. It is a flat arc that bends very slightly at the end, then snaps back. The arc is not transformation — she does not become warm or repentant — but it is a meaningful movement from purely closed to almost-cracked-open, ending with a retreat that itself says something.
character_arc.film_portrayal: The films do not trace this arc. The OotP crack (Dementor knowledge, Howler decision) is entirely absent. The HBP Dumbledore visit is absent. The DH farewell is present but brief and without the emotional scaffolding the books built across five volumes. In the films, Petunia is essentially the same character in DH Part 1 as she is in PS/SS: hostile, fearful, domestically obsessive. The farewell scene in the film does include Petunia's wet handkerchief and her failure to embrace Harry, which preserves the final beat's emotional ambiguity, but the audience has not seen any of the intermediate arc steps that give that beat weight.
character_arc.difference: The arc's intermediate steps — the OotP revelations, the Howler, the Dumbledore confrontation — are all absent. The starting and ending points are approximately correct (hostile in film 1, briefly ambiguous in film 7), but every meaningful step between is missing. The farewell in the film reads as a cold departure rather than a woman at the edge of a threshold she cannot cross, because the film has not established that she was ever close to crossing it.
character_arc.penalty_logic: The arc exists only at its endpoints in the films, with all the significant intermediate steps removed. This is more than compression — the intervening development is what gives the ending its meaning. Without it, the DH farewell is just a cold goodbye, not a near-moment. Score placed at 8: arc is incomplete and missing important steps, the ending is present but its dramatic logic has been gutted.

key_relationships.book_baseline: Petunia's most important relationships are: (1) with Harry — defined by hostility, fear, suppressed obligation, and occasional involuntary glimpses of something more complex; (2) with Lily — a ghost relationship of envy, resentment, love-denied, and regret that drives everything about her character; (3) with Vernon — she is usually subordinate but has moments of genuine authority (OotP: she overrides him on keeping Harry); (4) with Dumbledore — an implied prior arrangement that gives him some hold over her. The Harry-Petunia relationship is particularly important: there are brief moments in OotP (the Dementor scene, the Howler) where the relationship almost shifts, where Harry sees her as a frightened woman rather than simply a tormentor. The Lily relationship is the emotional core of everything Petunia is.
key_relationships.film_portrayal: The Harry-Petunia relationship in the films is one of pure hostility with no visible complexity. There is no scene equivalent to the OotP moments where Harry sees her differently. The DH farewell is present but telegraphed only by Petunia's tears over Dudley's unexpected kindness rather than any direct interaction with Harry. The Lily relationship is present in the PS/SS outburst and briefly in DH's Snape memory sequence, but the depth — the begging letter, the longing, the secret knowledge — is absent. The Dumbledore relationship is implied in the Howler but since the Howler scene is cut, it is functionally absent. The Vernon relationship is faithfully depicted as one of domestic partnership with Petunia occasionally subordinate and occasionally steadying him.
key_relationships.difference: The Lily relationship is the biggest loss: it is touched upon but never developed to the point where the audience understands that Petunia's entire characterisation is rooted in the wound of being the non-magical sister. The Harry relationship loses all its complexity: there is no film equivalent of the OotP moment where Harry sees her as 'his mother's sister' for the first time and understands what Voldemort's return means to her too. The Dumbledore relationship is entirely absent (its only trace — the Howler — is cut). The Vernon relationship is adequate.
key_relationships.penalty_logic: Two of Petunia's four key relationships lose most of their depth or disappear. The Lily relationship — which is the emotional foundation of her character — is sketched but not developed. The Dumbledore relationship is cut entirely. The Harry relationship loses the one moment in the books where it is meaningfully complicated. Score placed at 6: important relationship dynamics are altered or weakened, with the most foundational one (Lily) significantly underdeveloped.

complexity_nuance_lost_material.book_baseline: Book Petunia is a character of genuine complexity beneath a brittle surface: she is cruel but frightened; she enforces normalcy but secretly longed for magic; she despises Harry but is bound to him by a promise she cannot explain to Vernon; she is subordinate to Vernon but occasionally overrides him; she dismisses the wizarding world but has retained precise details about it for decades. The moments that reveal her complexity are: (1) the Dementor knowledge scene (OotP), (2) the Howler and her decision to keep Harry (OotP), (3) her wide-eyed fear when Harry says Voldemort is back (OotP), (4) the Dumbledore visit during which she is described as 'oddly flushed' by his rebuke (HBP), (5) young Petunia's longing and her letter to Dumbledore (backstory revealed in DH), (6) the farewell in which she nearly says something (DH). Each of these is a moment where the performed surface (hostile, normal, disgusted) cracks to show something underneath.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.film_portrayal: The films preserve the surface consistently — hostile domestic presence, Dudley-doting, anti-magic — but almost every moment of crack or complexity is absent. The Dementor knowledge scene is cut. The Howler decision is cut. The 'wide and fearful eyes' moment is cut. The Dumbledore rebuke scene is cut. The begging-letter backstory is absent. What the films do preserve is the PS/SS outburst (partial), the physical comedy of her panic at magical disturbances, and the DH farewell beat. The young Petunia in Snape's memories is present in two brief shots but does not convey the full weight of the backstory.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.difference: The films remove almost all material that complicates Petunia beyond hostile-Muggle-aunt. The audience has no access to the information that she secretly wanted to be a witch, that she has a prior arrangement with Dumbledore, that she knows wizarding world details she has suppressed for thirty years, or that there is a moment in OotP where Harry genuinely sees her as a person rather than a tormentor. Without these, film Petunia is a one-dimensional foil: unpleasant, comic in her terror, and narratively inert outside the PS/SS opening. This is a substantial flattening of a character the books establish as psychologically rich precisely because of what she hides.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.penalty_logic: The character is reduced to a simpler function — comic/hostile Muggle guardian — with almost none of the book material that made her genuinely complex. The flattening is not incidental: the removed scenes (Dementor knowledge, Howler decision, Dumbledore rebuke, farewell interiority) are specifically the scenes where the books do the most characterisation work on Petunia. Score placed at 7: major flattening, character reduced to a simpler function, though the surface traits are faithfully rendered.

OotP: The Howler from Dumbledore ('Remember my last, Petunia') and Petunia's decision to override Vernon and keep Harry — entirely cut from the films
OotP: The moment Harry sees Petunia's 'wide and fearful' eyes and recognises her as his mother's sister for the first time — cut from the films

DH backstory: The platform scene in which young Petunia's contempt for Hogwarts is revealed as a cover for desperate exclusion — absent

The implication that Petunia's keeping of Harry was an active obligation she chose in response to Dumbledore's prior communication — never established in the films

Cap 2 (80): Applied — Petunia's key relationships (Lily, Harry, Dumbledore) are substantially changed or absent, capping total below 80

Cap 5 (60): Borderline — motivations are not incoherent but are substantially flattened; the most important internal conflict (prior arrangement with Dumbledore, suppressed longing for magic) is absent. Total lands just above 60 because the surface characterisation is genuinely faithful and the existing film material is not wrong, only incomplete
comparative.key_observations: Film Petunia is a faithful surface rendering of an unfaithful characterisation. The brittle, hostile, Dudley-adoring, magic-fearing domestic tyrant is consistently and accurately portrayed across all eight films. Her voice, physical mannerisms, clipped speech, and reactive terror at magical disturbances are all recognisably book-authentic. But virtually every scene that makes Petunia interesting — that reveals the envious, frightened, secretly-knowing woman beneath the performance — is absent. The Howler decision (her single most agentic book moment), the Dementor knowledge revelation (her most psychologically complex moment), the Dumbledore rebuke (which gives her arc its moral weight), and the backstory of her letter to Hogwarts (the foundation of her entire characterisation) are all cut. What remains is a character who is recognisable but has been reduced from a psychologically layered minor figure to a reliable source of comic hostility. The total of 61 reflects a portrayal that is accurate in everything it shows but has lost the material that gave the character depth, agency, and complexity.
